content: The National Tuberculosis Programs (NTPs) can gain critical insights into their tuberculosis (TB) surveillance systems through the evaluation of specific benchmarks. For countries lacking Vital Registration (VR) data, the assessment of benchmarks 2 to 7 relies on the analysis of available data and expert opinion to interpret the results. Expert opinion is essential in these cases because universally applicable quantitative tests for internal data consistency have not yet been established. Even in countries with high-performing surveillance systems, the internal consistency of data is often evaluated based on expert judgment. To ensure objectivity, the determination of whether benchmarks are met should involve at least two independent assessors, with input from the NTP. If all parties agree that the data convincingly demonstrate that the core benchmarks are satisfied, the standard can be considered met. For countries with VR data, the VR benchmark is satisfied if trends in TB case notification rates and TB mortality rates do not move in opposite directions. If the VR benchmark is satisfied, the standard is met. For countries without VR data, all five benchmarks (or six, if presumptive TB data are available) must be satisfied to meet the standard. A benchmark can still be satisfied if data inconsistencies are explainable. For example, a significant but explainable year-to-year decline in case notifications that reflects a true decline satisfies the benchmark. However, if a dramatic change in the sex ratio of cases is due to reporting errors, such as staff failing to submit reports, this inconsistency is considered a surveillance artifact rather than a true change, and the benchmark is not satisfied. These explanations should be documented in a checklist. If only some benchmarks are satisfied, the standard is partially met. If no benchmarks are satisfied, the standard is not met. When trends are inconsistent, countries should investigate the reasons behind these inconsistencies. Rapid changes over time or inconsistent trends in case reports should be examined for errors and corrected at all levels, including source data verification. Recent changes in the coverage of routine TB surveillance may explain opposing trends in TB cases and deaths, and this possibility should be explored. Differences may also reflect true variations in the TB epidemic over time or across sub-national regions, influenced by factors such as HIV prevalence, urbanization, socioeconomic conditions, or the effectiveness of TB control activities. If necessary, key actions to address benchmark gaps should be described, along with an estimated budget to support these activities. The adjusted mortality rate for selected years should only include countries where the data source is classified as VR or VR imputed. However, VR data are still unavailable in approximately 100 countries. For example, in the 2012 Global Tuberculosis Report, direct measurements of mortality trends from VR systems were available for only 119 out of 217 countries and territories. In countries without VR systems, it has not been possible to define standardized quantitative tests for internal consistency that are universally applicable. Since each country is at a different stage of the TB epidemic, setting a standardized limit for internal consistency variation is not feasible. Therefore, expert opinion is used to interpret analysis results and determine whether the standard is met. Alternative methods used by other countries to ensure and improve the internal consistency of national TB surveillance data are documented elsewhere. For countries with VR data, if trends in case notification rates and TB mortality rates move in opposite directions, the VR benchmark is not satisfied. If the VR benchmark is satisfied, the standard is met. For countries without VR data, all five benchmarks (or six, if presumptive TB data are available) must be satisfied to meet the standard. A benchmark can be satisfied if data inconsistencies are explainable. For example, a dramatic but explainable year-to-year decline in case notifications that reflects a true decline satisfies the benchmark. However, if a dramatic change in the sex ratio of cases is due to reporting errors, such as staff failing to submit reports, this inconsistency is considered a surveillance artifact rather than a true change, and the benchmark is not satisfied. These explanations should be documented in a checklist. If only some benchmarks are satisfied, the standard is partially met. If no benchmarks are satisfied, the standard is not met. When trends are inconsistent, countries should investigate the reasons behind these inconsistencies. Rapid changes over time or inconsistent trends in case reports should be examined for errors and corrected at all levels, including source data verification. Recent changes in the coverage of routine TB surveillance may explain opposing trends in TB cases and deaths, and this possibility should be explored. Differences may also reflect true variations in the TB epidemic over time or across sub-national regions, influenced by factors such as HIV prevalence, urbanization, socioeconomic conditions, or the effectiveness of TB control activities. If necessary, key actions to address benchmark gaps should be described, along with an estimated budget to support these activities. The ratio of notified pulmonary TB (PTB) to extrapulmonary TB (EPTB) cases is another important benchmark. Data for the total number of PTB and EPTB cases reported nationally over the previous five years are required. All new and relapsed TB cases should be included in the analysis. The ratio of PTB to EPTB cases should be calculated for each year. For example, in Uganda, the ratio of PTB to EPTB cases was generally consistent, with a slight increase in pulmonary cases during 2010 and 2011, suggesting good internal consistency. This benchmark was considered satisfied. If data are available, this analysis may also be conducted at the sub-national level. The ratio of male to female TB cases is another benchmark. Data for the total number of notified TB cases reported nationally for males and females over the previous five years are required. All new and relapsed TB cases should be included in the analysis. The ratio of male to female TB cases should be calculated for each year. For example, in Uganda, the male-to-female ratio of notified TB cases was generally consistent between 2008 and 2012, but there was a notable increase in the proportion of male cases over time. This trend could suggest that women were less likely to seek healthcare or were underdiagnosed, that men became more likely to seek healthcare, or that there was a real epidemiological increase in TB among men. This benchmark was deemed satisfied, but further investigation into the increasing ratio is recommended. The proportion of childhood TB cases out of all TB cases is another benchmark. Data for the total number of nationally notified childhood TB cases (ages 0–14) and the total number of all notified TB cases (any age) over the previous five years are required. In Uganda, data were only available for new smear-positive childhood TB cases. The proportion of smear-positive childhood TB cases out of all smear-positive TB cases was calculated for each year. Although the proportion of children reported to have smear-positive TB decreased over time, there was a larger decline between 2008 and 2009, followed by an increase in 2010. This variation requires further investigation, and this benchmark was not deemed satisfied. The year-to-year change in the case notification rate for all forms of TB is another benchmark. National case notification rates for all forms of TB over the previous five years are required, along with national population data for each year. In Uganda, data showed a decline in TB case notification rates at the national level between 2008 and 2012. However, the percentage change in TB case notification rates at the national level showed significant variability by year, suggesting that the data are not internally consistent. This benchmark was not satisfied. The analysis can also be conducted at the sub-national level if notification and population data are available. In Uganda, TB notification rates were compared by geographical zone from 2008 to 2012. The percentage change in TB case notification rates at the sub-national level showed significant variability over time and by reporting region, highlighting areas that require further investigation and intervention. The ratio of people with presumptive TB to total notifications of TB cases is another benchmark. Data for the number of people with presumptive TB and the number of new and relapsed TB cases (all forms) are required. Ideally, people with presumptive TB include all those suspected of having TB, regardless of whether a smear or other laboratory test was performed. The ratio of TB suspects to notifications can be calculated for each year. In Uganda, the ratio of people with presumptive TB to notifications increased steadily between 2008 and 2012. These trends satisfy the benchmark requirement for consistency and suggest that the reach of the NTP is steadily expanding. However, despite an increase in the number of tests performed over time, the number of notified cases did not increase at the same rate and even declined in 2012 compared with 2011. Further investigations may reveal changes in laboratory testing methods, case definitions, or other artifacts of the surveillance system. In summary, for countries without VR data, benchmarks 2 to 7 were applied in this assessment. Data trends were evaluated for internal consistency and to determine whether the benchmarks were satisfied.
